b: p
Phil Collen has looked back on his surprising switch to heavy guitar strings – and revealed it was Gary Moore who set him on his path to conversion.
p

The Def Leppard guitarist is a proponent of fretboard pyro. He plays a high-performance signature twist on the Jackson Dinky, and those US Custom Shop builds have all the luxuries to make them easy to play.
p

Collen can play a ripping solo with the best of them. But he likes a guitar that fights back. The production models of his PC-1 signature guitar – most recently reimagined as the pre-relic’d PC1-E Mexican-built Pro Series model – have skinny necks as per the brand’s house style, and yet Collen will get his tech to find him baseball bat necks.
p

Those signatures also ship with 9-gauge strings, but Collen puts 13s on his own. In the new issue of Guitarist, Collen explains exactly why he likes heavy electric guitar strings – and it all goes back to his early touring adventures with Def Leppard, when one of his all-time heroes was opening the show for them.
p

“Back on Def Leppard’s Pyromania tour, Gary Moore was opening for us,” recalls Collen. “I went into his dressing room and saw the famous Peter Green Les Paul. I said, ‘Is that the Peter Green Les Paul?’ and Gary said, ‘Yeah, do you want to play it?’ So he picked up another guitar and we jammed for about an hour.”
p
This was a real pinch-me moment for Collen. It was also life changing. Greeny was working its magic on him, and he liked how Moore had set the guitar up.
p
“He had 10s on the Les Paul – I was used to playing nines, but I loved the feel,” says Collen.
p

Collen duly started using 10s. But that’s the funny thing about the guitar; you start going down the rabbit-hole, and you keep going deeper. The heavier gauge strings allowed him to express himself better.
p

“I use 13s to 54s now,” says Collen. “After a while I moved up to 11s, then 12s and eventually 13s. I’ve probably been using 13s for about 10 years now. Your fingers get stronger, and I like being able to really lay into the guitar.”
p
Collen isn’t the first high-profile player to use heavy strings on his electric guitar. Stevie Ray Vaughan was the most-famous proponent of strings like power cables.
p

Malcolm Young liked a set of 12s, and the Edge and Joe Bonamassa string up with a set of 11s, which is still pretty heavy – and it feels like a bigger step up from nines to 10s. Jim Adkins of Jimmy Eat World uses 13s, as does Bonamassa’s rhythm guitarist and co-producer Josh Smith.
p
And if you think these guys are nuts, then just consider Dick Dale. He used a set of 16s.
p
You can read this Phil Collen interview in full in the latest issue of Guitarist – better still, save and subscribe.
